question: What closed-form, gradient-free procedures exist for choosing, synthesising or moving KEYS in a fixed-size associative store so that a new write is retrievable by new queries without destroying retrieval of the old content? And is there a principled reason to expect a key-side write to preserve QA better or worse than the measured value-side alternatives, or is 'keys collapse QA' untested folklore in our setting?
variable_under_test: none (literature scout + no-GPU internal mining; no source file modified)
baseline_ref: DIAG-ROUTING (rho_MT=0.012, QA/MT routing cosine 0.99899, top-32 overlap 0.914) and ORACLE-WRITE (mass_on_S MT 0.0896 / QA 0.0827, ratio 1.04; MT 2.381 ceiling at 9% bandwidth)

numbers.note: No GPU run, no training, no eval. All quantitative results below are (a) re-analysis of the existing research_loop/state/diagnostics/DIAG-ROUTING.npz on CPU, (b) closed-form arithmetic on already-measured scalars, or (c) facts read out of source files and config.json. No number here is new GPU measurement.

central_algebraic_result_beta_vs_key.statement: A per-key additive logit bias (beta) is query-INDEPENDENT, so it maps mass_on_S(MT) and mass_on_S(QA) through the same monotone map m(delta)=m0*e^d/(m0*e^d+1-m0) and drives the MT/QA ratio toward 1. Only a key change can be asymmetric, because its logit contribution q.dk/sqrt(d) is query-DEPENDENT.
central_algebraic_result_beta_vs_key.consequence: The AM paper's box beta in [-3,3] (LIT-002) is by itself sufficient to take mass_on_S from 0.090 to ~0.66 -- i.e. the bandwidth problem is solvable by beta alone -- but it CANNOT change the MT/QA ratio of 1.04. Separation requires keys.
central_algebraic_result_beta_vs_key.key_side_bound: Delta_MT - Delta_QA = (qbar_MT - qbar_QA).dk/sqrt(d) <= ||dk||*||qbar_MT - qbar_QA||/sqrt(d). The whole key-side lever is proportional to ||qbar_MT - qbar_QA|| in the 128-dim per-head QUERY space, which this loop has never measured.

reproduction_check.note: reproduces DIAG-ROUTING headline numbers exactly from mean_routing_qa/mean_routing_mt

new_1_routing_difference_norm.definition: ||abar_MT - abar_QA|| / ||abar_MT|| per (layer,head) over the 512-slot routing simplex
new_1_routing_difference_norm.reading: the two tasks' mean routing differs by ~5% relative. Combined with the QA routing Gram's participation effective rank of 1.97 (DIAG-ROUTING), this is evidence that the incumbent 512 keys resolve queries into ~2 effective directions -- i.e. KEY BLINDNESS -- not evidence that the query populations are aligned in R^128.

new_2_sink_slot.reading: one slot per layer owns >half the cartridge routing mass and is shared across heads in 29/36 layers. Any key rewrite that evicts it is an attention-sink deletion (LIT-021).

new_3_routing_entropy.reading: 40-43 effective addresses out of 512 (8%). Kanerva/SDM coverage condition (LIT-023) is violated.

written_support_S_size_per_layer.source: ORACLE-WRITE_route_mass.json runs['phase1_oracleS|MT'].n_slots_per_layer (union over 16 documents of the per-layer tf-idf top-32)

new_4_selector_bandwidth_gap.gap: 4.6x more cartridge mass available at a SMALLER slot budget (32 vs ~55)
new_4_selector_bandwidth_gap.leading_hypothesis: cartridges/am/query_accum.py:87-89 builds the access scores used for slot selection from a GQA-group MEAN query (q_grouped.mean(dim=2), 4 query heads averaged BEFORE the softmax). softmax(mean(q)) is not mean(softmax(q)); post-RoPE query heads within a group are near-unrelated directions, so their mean is a small, near-random vector and the resulting 'attention mass' is not the mass any head actually places. Falsifier (one forward pass, zero solves): recompute access scores per KV head without pooling and compare the top-32 index sets against the pooled ones.
new_4_selector_bandwidth_gap.caveat: This is a hypothesis from reading, not a measurement. A second candidate (per-document variation of the selection) is not excluded, though it points the wrong way: the union has MORE slots than 32 and still carries less mass. Note also SLOT_SELECTION=attention_mass already exists (ranking.py:22) but consumes the SAME pooled access scores, so it would not fix this.

H2_missing_counter_rotation_on_key_rewri.finding: key_select.py::rewrite_keys_on_support scores candidates with doc_key_start/doc_rope_offset set (:258-278) and then installs the RAW selected key into a cartridge slot (:283) with no RoPE re-basing. phase1.py::_rope_reposition (:42-68) implements exactly the missing R_delta and initial_am_compaction.py:150 already uses it (rebake_key_positions).
H2_missing_counter_rotation_on_key_rewri.consequence: The first-ever KEY_MODE != freeze run would measure a phase-corrupted key, not a key mechanism.

H3_frame_bookkeeping.finding: cartridge keys baked at positions 0..511 (initialization/text.py:45); doc keys baked at 0..T_doc-1 (teacher.py::prefill_document_kv_cache called at continual.py:162 with default position_offset=0; the Phase-1 logs' own rope_note confirms 'Per-doc prefill at position 0 ... absolute RoPE positions overlap'); reference and eval queries at arange(seq_len) from 0 (utils/chat.py:70, generation.py:228). In that convention doc and cartridge keys are already in a COMMON frame, yet finetune.py:495 applies a T_doc query rotation anyway.

H4_operational_blocker_for_the_cheapest_.finding: finetune.py:264-269 _should_fit_beta returns key_mode != 'freeze' when enable_beta is None, and continual_am_sparse.py:104-109 maps an UNSET ENABLE_BETA to None. So KEY_MODE=highest_attention with ENABLE_BETA unset silently enables the beta/NNLS path that crashed EXP-005 (cholesky not-PD), EXP-005b (NaN in ridge lstsq) and EXP-006 (NaN inside refit_beta_nnls).
H4_operational_blocker_for_the_cheapest_.workaround_no_code_change: ENABLE_BETA=0 forces _should_fit_beta -> False at :267-268 while leaving key_mode free, giving a clean keys-only arm.

observations: Nine LIT entries (LIT-019..LIT-027) were written, all with predictions about our measured signatures; none is marked unusable. The organising result is algebraic, not bibliographic: a per-key logit bias (beta) is query-independent, so it maps mass_on_S(MT) and mass_on_S(QA) through the same monotone map and drives the measured MT/QA ratio from 1.083 toward 1.006 as it raises bandwidth; the only term that can be asymmetric is a key change, whose asymmetry is bounded by ||qbar_MT - qbar_QA|| in the 128-dim per-head query space. That norm has never been measured in this loop; DIAG-ROUTING measured its 512-dim routing-space shadow instead. Re-analysing DIAG-ROUTING.npz on CPU, that shadow is ||abar_MT - abar_QA||/||abar_MT|| = 0.053, but the QA routing Gram has participation effective rank 1.97 -- the incumbent keys project every query onto about two effective directions, so a 0.914 top-32 overlap is evidence of key blindness rather than of query similarity, and rho_MT = 0.012 is an upper bound set by what those keys can resolve, not by the queries. The same npz yields three previously unrecorded facts: one slot per layer carries 52.5% of cartridge routing mass and is the same slot for all 8 KV heads in 29 of 36 layers; routing entropy is 2.81/2.89 nats, i.e. 40-43 effective addresses of 512, which violates the SDM coverage condition that licenses value-only writing into fixed keys; and the tf-idf written support (mean 54.7 slots per layer, from ORACLE-WRITE_route_mass.json) carries 15.2% of cartridge mass where a mass-ranked per-layer top-32 would carry 70.4% -- a 4.6x bandwidth gap at a smaller slot budget, whose leading cause by reading is that the access scores driving slot selection are built from a GQA-group MEAN query before the softmax (query_accum.py:87-89). Four code hazards were found by reading and are recorded in diagnostics: rope_theta is hard-coded to 10000.0 everywhere in cartridges/am while the model uses 5,000,000, and it is live in the teacher-target path of every AM run at offsets (T_doc = 3858-8900) where the two rotations are fully decorrelated (E[cos] 0.24-0.34 at 1-2k, 0.00 at 4k; 75% of dimension pairs off by more than 1 radian at offset 1024); rewrite_keys_on_support installs a selected document key into a cartridge slot with no counter-rotation, although phase1.py::_rope_reposition implements exactly that operator and initial_am_compaction.py already calls it; the cartridge, document and query position frames are already common under this repo's arange-from-0 convention, yet finetune.py:495 applies a T_doc query rotation anyway; and _should_fit_beta silently switches on the broken beta/NNLS path whenever KEY_MODE != freeze with ENABLE_BETA unset, which would make the first key experiment fail for a B-SOLVE reason. On the question asked directly: there is no principled reason from the literature to expect a key write to preserve QA better or worse per se -- the published evidence says a key write trades eviction for reachability, and every mechanism that succeeds (ROME's prefix-averaged k*, Kaiser's K[n'] <- q at the least-recently-used slot, DNC's allocation weighting, SDM's fixed random addresses) writes the key AT the new query and places it where the old content is NOT read. The pre-loop claim 'keys collapse QA' is untested folklore in this setting: every row in results.csv is KEY_MODE=freeze, and the two confounds that would have produced that observation are present in our code independently of key geometry -- the candidate pool offers up exactly the highest-QA-mass slots (0.914 overlap) including the layer sink, and the installed key carries a multi-thousand-position rotary phase error. RANKING of key-side mechanisms by likelihood of raising the MT/QA mass ratio above 1.04 without pushing QA past 2.52: (1) LIT-024 usage/LRU allocation -- SLOT_SELECTION=qa_least_used combined with KEY_MODE=query_centroid (k* = c*qbar_MT/||qbar_MT||) is the only candidate that raises the ratio on both factors at once, is the cheapest of all of them, and is the published rule rather than a synthesis; (2) LIT-020 null-space key placement in Q0 (k* = c*P_perp*qbar_MT), which is strictly stronger but is gated on rho_key being large and needs one new 19 MB statistic; (3) LIT-019 ROME-style doc-centroid key synthesis, which should raise mass_on_S but has no orthogonality term and so may raise the level without the ratio; (4) LIT-021 key-norm scaling, which raises mass_on_S continuously but is beta in disguise unless combined with (1) or (2); (5) LIT-025 selection-only variants, which are bounded above at a ratio of about 1.2 by the measured 0.914 overlap. CHEAPEST DISCRIMINATING EXPERIMENT: rho_key -- the key-space analogue of DIAG-ROUTING's rho -- computed as tr(P_perp_r Q0_MT)/tr(Q0_MT) from the 128x128 per-head query second moments Q0_QA and Q0_MT, using the same forward-pass hooks and the same two eval splits DIAG-ROUTING already used (it collected 49152 QA and 40960 MT query rows per head in 5.7 s of collection, 86 s wall-clock total), 288 tiny EVDs, 19 MB of storage, no solve and no eval. It costs a fraction of DIAG-ROUTING and it decides the entire key family in one number: rho_key << 0.05 means MT and QA queries are the same direction in R^128, no key placement can be asymmetric, and B-ROUTE closes confirmed+capped for keys as well as values; rho_key in [0.15, 0.6] means the axes are separable in key space and mechanisms (1)-(3) are live. The cheapest experiment that reuses an existing flag is KEY_MODE=highest_attention ENABLE_BETA=0 AM_ORACLE_WRITE=0 at the canonical top_t=32 -- env-only, no code change, never run -- but its interpretation is confounded by hazards H2 (missing rope re-basing) and by sink eviction, so it measures the folklore rather than the mechanism unless run as the three-arm control set in LIT-027.
